newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa partially postpones tax perk crackdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa partially postpones tax perk crackdown.

text.p: In a landmark development, the South African parliamentary finance committee has persuaded the finance ministry to amend a money bill aimed at cracking down on tax perks on employer-owned housing.

A spokeswoman confirmed on Tuesday that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Deputy Finance Minister Gill Marcus had agreed to postpone planned action against salary sacrifice housing schemes but would still act against more "aggressive" housing tax perks this year.

As a bill affecting revenue, the bill is classed as a money bill and parliament normally would not be allowed to amend it. This is the first time that it has been able to persuade the ministry to do so.
The finance committee, which has had extensive public hearings on the proposed clampdown, last week decided to appeal to the ministry to amend the bill.

Committee members said that although they accepted that the tax breaks on employer-owned housing had been abused by some wealthy individuals, the proposed new taxes would mostly affect middle to lower class employees.

It would also be unfair in that it would mean that those employees housed in company-owned accommodation would be taxed less than those living in houses rented by their companies, even though they earned the same salaries.

According to Deputy Commissioner of Revenue Kosie Louw, abuses had included cases where employers had sold their homes to trusts or other schemes which they essentially controlled, but which had been used to benefit from lower taxes.
Others were so called "salary sacrifice" schemes which were not illegal but had become such a standard practice it had to act.
"It was definitely starting to have an effect on the tax base," Louw said.
The ministry spokeswoman said that Marcus had informed the committee on Tuesday that some changes would be made to the bill before it was tabled in parliament on Thursday.

"Action against salary sacrifice schemes will be postponed to March 1998 but the government still finds them unacceptable and employers and employees should use this period to make alternative arrangements," she said.
"Where employees retain an interest in the accommodation, which is viewed as aggressive avoidance, government will still act against them this year."
She said the South African Revenue Services would release further details later this week.

The bill, which aims to plug a wide range of tax loopholes, will put in place several anti-tax avoidance measures announced in his March 12 budget by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, who is abroad at the moment.
